say.text: One-pager time. First a retrieval gate: eight quick recalls, no teaching yet.
Answer from memory. Whatever you miss goes onto the page we build at the end.
Complete the line: TOF is the most common ___ congenital heart disease, and its picture varies with the ___.
Which pair?
Yes. TOF is the most common cyanotic CHD, and presentation varies with the severity of RVOT obstruction.

Tempting, because the VSD is the biggest hole you can see in the heart. But the line says the picture varies with the **RVOT obstruction**, and TOF is the most common **cyanotic** CHD. Obstruction, not the hole, sets the blueness.
Tempting, since some TOF children are barely blue. But the most common **cyanotic** CHD is TOF, and its presentation varies with the severity of RVOT obstruction.
Which of these is one of the four components of classic TOF?
Right. RV hypertrophy is the fourth component; ASD, PDA and LVH are not among the four.
An ASD is tempting because it is another septal hole beside the VSD. Think about the four: one hole, one valve-level problem, one vessel position, one muscle change. Does a second hole fit?

say.text: Second look. Same question.
Which of these is one of the four components of classic TOF?
The four components: a **large, anteriorly malaligned VSD**, an **overriding aorta**, **infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction** and **right ventricular hypertrophy**.
ASD, PDA and LVH are the keyed distractors in the 'not part of TOF' PYQs.
Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus which lesion?
Yes. Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus an ASD.
A PDA is tempting because it is the usual extra lesion you meet in cyanotic hearts. Think of the other septum, not a vessel.

Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus which lesion?
**Pentalogy of Fallot** = TOF plus an **atrial septal defect**; the term is old and seldom used now.
Exam note: pentalogy is the fifth-lesion question, and the answer is ASD.

choices.label: Chest X-ray showing a boot-shaped heart

say.text: The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary diagnostic modality.
The chest X-ray may classically show a **boot-shaped** heart with an upturned apex from RV hypertrophy: a sign, not the confirmatory test.
A TOF child is in a hypercyanotic spell. You place the child knee-chest. Why?

choices.label: It helps diurese the congested lungs

say.text: Yes. Knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance.
Lowering resistance is tempting, because vasodilation helps many failing hearts. But think about which way the blood is shunting in a spell and what would push it back toward the lungs.

say.text: A diuretic is tempting if you file this as heart failure. Ask whether the lungs are congested or starved of flow.

A TOF child is in a hypercyanotic spell. You place the child knee-chest. Why?

choices.label: It helps diurese the congested lungs

say.text: **Knee-chest positioning** is done to increase systemic vascular resistance. Together with oxygen to cause pulmonary vasodilation, fluid boluses to improve RV filling and IV phenylephrine to increase systemic afterload, every step pushes blood toward the lungs.
Next spell step: IV phenylephrine. Its job?

choices.label: Reduce afterload so the heart can empty
Treat the heart failure behind the spell

say.text: Right. IV phenylephrine increases systemic afterload. IV beta-blockers decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further.
Tempting, because afterload reduction is the usual move in a failing heart. A spell is the opposite problem. The step is **IV phenylephrine**, to **increase systemic afterload**.
Tempting, because a sick blue child looks like heart failure. But phenylephrine's job is **to increase systemic afterload**, not to treat failure.
Repaired TOF, years later. What is the most common indication for reoperation?
Yes. Pulmonary insufficiency is the commonest reason to go back in.
Residual VSD is tempting: you closed it, so you expect it to leak. Think instead about what the outflow repair does to the pulmonary valve.

Repaired TOF, years later. What is the most common indication for reoperation?
**Pulmonary insufficiency** is the most common indication for reoperation after repair.
Without surgery, what is the most frequent cause of death in TOF?
Right. Most frequent causes of death without surgery: hypoxic spells (68%), cerebrovascular accidents (17%), brain abscesses (13%).
A real cause, so tempting, but second place. In unrepaired TOF: hypoxic spells 68%, cerebrovascular accidents 17%, brain abscesses 13%.

say.text: Every step on the line should push blood toward the lungs. Which option has steps that do that?

Yes: **knee-chest** to increase SVR, **oxygen** for pulmonary vasodilation, **IV fluids** to improve RV filling, **IV beta-blockers** to decrease heart rate, **IV phenylephrine** to increase systemic afterload, **morphine** as sedative.
Tempting if you treat the spell as failure. But the steps raise systemic resistance (knee-chest, phenylephrine) and aid RV filling (fluids, beta-blockers).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: afterload goes up, not down, in a spell.

Most common cyanotic CHD: TOF; reoperation: residual VSD; gold standard: boot-shaped X-ray

say.text: That is the page: TOF most common cyanotic CHD, echocardiogram the gold standard, pulmonary insufficiency the commonest reoperation indication.
Tempting, since residual VSD and the boot sign are both classic TOF words. But reoperation is mostly for **pulmonary insufficiency**, and the gold standard is the **echocardiogram**.
